results.name: A Dish Served Lukewarm: The Refrigerator Botnet
results.description: Exposed Dixell/Copeland XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers are being exploited as abuse infrastructure. The STRIKE Team discovered a suspected SMTP botnet comprising nine IP addresses, with three confirmed as refrigeration controllers. These devices, used in supermarkets and cold storage facilities, remain exposed on the internet with unpatched vulnerabilities, particularly CVE-2026-25085. Attackers are repurposing these controllers as tunnel gateways, residential-proxy exits, and spam senders. Analysis revealed outbound-only SMTP traffic with significant target-list overlap among nodes, indicating coordinated operations. Of 1,041 mail targets, 508 were hit by multiple nodes, with the three most active sharing approximately 47% of their targets. The exposed controllers carry vulnerable firmware and lack security monitoring, making them ideal for prolonged malicious use without detection.

results.name: ARTEX: Agentic Asbestos
results.description: ARTEX is an open-source, LLM-driven autonomous penetration testing framework released in July 2026 that integrates AI agents with reconnaissance and exploitation capabilities. As of November 2026, 1,465 hosts run exposed ARTEX consoles globally, with approximately 815 distinct deployments. CrowdStrike linked ARTEX usage to attacks against South Korean financial institutions, while Microsoft attributed its use to Storm-0940's ConnectWise supply chain compromise. The framework enables automated operations from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with minimal human intervention. Ten percent of ARTEX hosts also run other offensive tools including Cobalt Strike, Vshell, and additional AI attack frameworks. Operators frequently expose open directories containing exploit binaries, post-exploitation kits, and session histories. The tool's developer claimed it was intended for authorized testing and took the repository offline after public attribution, though archived copies remain circulating.

results.name: Email threat landscape: Q3 2026 trends and insights
results.description: From July through September 2026, approximately 7.3 billion email-based phishing threats were detected, with September reaching nearly 3 billion attacks—a 41% increase from August. The quarter demonstrated significant shifts in attack techniques, including a sharp decline in QR code phishing, a recovery in CAPTCHA-gated attacks driven by SVG attachments, and persistent domain spoofing affecting 129 million messages impersonating business services. Credential theft remained the dominant objective across malicious attachments, while business contact impersonation declined and Teams-based threats increasingly used ordinary personal names rather than explicit help desk identities. Notable campaigns targeted legal organizations with personalized salary review lures leading to device code phishing, and Spanish-speaking users with purchase order and payroll themes delivering Agent Tesla malware. The disruption of Tycoon2FA phishing platform continued showing effectiveness with 99.8% volume reduction.

results.name: Iranian State-Aligned Threat Actor Masquerading as Dubai Airports IT Department Delivering Trojanized Coding Challenges - Blinder Tunnel Campaign Targeting Iraqi Critical Infrastructure
results.description: An Iranian state-aligned threat actor designated as CL-STA-1178 has been impersonating the Dubai Airports IT department to deliver trojanized coding challenges to high-value targets. The Blinder Tunnel campaign, active since November 2025 with attacks intensifying in March 2026, primarily targeted Iraqi critical infrastructure. The operation employs a three-step attack chain exploiting legitimate Windows developer files, AppDomainManager hijacking, and DLL sideloading to deploy ShelbyLoader V2 malware. Attackers abuse GitHub API infrastructure for command-and-control communications, utilizing repositories for decryption keys, payload downloads, and GitHub issues as fallback mechanisms. The campaign incorporates Peaky Blinders television show themes in its infrastructure naming and embeds the show's theme song in malware. Operational security failures exposed connections to a separate credential harvesting operation targeting Israeli entities using conflict-themed Google Drive lures during May-June 2026.

results.name: Akira Ransomware Attack Investigation
results.description: In September, an organization experienced an Akira ransomware attack, with investigation revealing the threat actor's tactics and tools. The attacker gained access through Remote Desktop Protocol, subsequently disabling antivirus protections on the compromised endpoint. The adversary deployed Rclone for data exfiltration purposes and utilized a GOST tunneling tool to maintain persistence within the network. Following these preparatory activities, the ransomware payload was executed. Forensic analysis of the impacted endpoints enabled investigators to identify key indicators of compromise, including command and control infrastructure and malicious executables. The investigation uncovered specific file paths and SHA256 hashes associated with the ransomware binary and GOST tunnel executable, along with the C2 server IP address used for tunnel communications.

results.name: Attackers Target AI Development Platform Langflow
results.description: In September 2026, F5 Labs detected 405 exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-0768, an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Langflow AI application-building platform, originating from 55 distinct IP addresses. This marks the first observation of an AI/ML development platform RCE in opportunistic internet-wide scanning. Captured payloads included capability probing with unique markers, timing-based execution checks, and environment harvesting attempts aimed at extracting cloud credentials, model API keys, and database secrets. Activity came primarily from two infrastructure clusters: Google Cloud hosts using environment-harvesting payloads with forged AI-crawler User-Agents, and European scanning subnets employing marker-based capability probing with spoofed localhost headers. results.name: From Streaming to Stealing: Mirax and the Rise of Server-side Android Device Takeover in META
results.description: Between March and September 2026, thousands of Android devices in the META region were infected with Mirax malware, causing millions in estimated losses. The campaign uses malicious advertisements within low-reputation streaming apps on Google Play to distribute droppers installing the payload. Mirax impersonates Google Play Services using Cyrillic characters and coerces victims into granting Accessibility Service permissions, enabling complete device takeover. The malware employs server-side configuration with dual-WebSocket C2 infrastructure, DNS-over-HTTPS, and dynamically pushed phishing templates targeting over 20 regional banks and digital wallets. Attackers perform real-time remote control to execute unauthorized transactions appearing legitimate, with funds transferred to suspected mule accounts in India. Activity peaked during Eid holidays and remains ongoing.

results.name: CWPdoor: The Invisible Backdoor Living Inside Control Web Panel
results.description: A sophisticated passive backdoor named cwpdoor has been discovered targeting Control Web Panel (CWP), a free open-source server management control panel for Linux. The malware embeds malicious code directly into the legitimate cwpsrv binary and is triggered only by specially crafted HTTP requests containing cryptographic signatures. It executes commands remotely while suppressing access logs, leaving no forensic traces. With over 340,000 CWP instances exposed to the internet, the threat surface is substantial. First observed in June 2026 with deployment infrastructure at 136.0.141.71, the backdoor achieved zero detection rates across security vendors. A real-world victim was identified in Brazil in September 2026. The backdoor uses RSA signature verification and AES-256-CBC encryption for command and control communications through Unix domain sockets, making detection extremely difficult through conventional means.

results.name: New Lindnor Backdoor and Glut of Security Killers Used in Ransomware Attack on U.S. Org
results.description: Attackers leveraging Anubis ransomware targeted a U.S. organization in October 2026, deploying a previously undocumented custom backdoor named Lindnor. The backdoor masqueraded as Chrome and VMware components on Microsoft SQL Server machines. Within approximately one hour, threat actors dropped at least 13 executables designed to terminate security services, utilizing five publicly known vulnerable drivers through Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) techniques. The attackers installed AnyDesk remote access tool with Safe Mode persistence capabilities to maintain access when security software was not fully operational. Despite deploying numerous security evasion tools and establishing multiple persistence mechanisms, the file encryption payload was successfully blocked before execution. Anubis ransomware, operated by the Hawkmoth group as a ransomware-as-a-service operation, has claimed approximately 96 victims over the past year, with 52% located in the United States.

results.name: Inside Phexia: A macOS malware delivered through ClickFix
results.description: Phexia is a modular macOS backdoor and infostealer actively distributed through ClickFix campaigns since late 2025. The malware employs a multi-stage infection chain beginning with Terminal command execution that downloads shell scripts, establishes persistence via LaunchAgents, and deploys AppleScript-based loaders. A significant evolution occurred in May 2026 when operators began using Polygon blockchain smart contracts as command-and-control dead-drop resolvers, replacing earlier Telegram and Steam-based methods. Post-compromise activities include credential harvesting through fake password prompts, browser data theft, keychain extraction, password manager targeting, and XMRig cryptominer deployment. The malware collects login passwords, browser encryption keys, cookies, and cryptocurrency wallet information. Multiple distinct builds communicate with rotating infrastructure, with reinfection potentially leaving concurrent installations active on compromised endpoints.
